channel.title: Family Dinner Plan
channel.description: A few minutes every Saturday walking through the coming week's family dinners: what's cooking each night and one quick tip per meal.
channel.itunes:author: Meal Planner Bot

item.title: Week of September 12, 2026
item.description:
BENDY: This week we are slow-cooking, stir-frying, and roasting one piece of pork that will make your Sunday smell like a wood-fired bakery, but the real trick is the game plan we set today.
BUB: We're going to a farmer's market and a grocery store before I even finish my cartoons, aren't we.
BENDY: You know it. Today is prep day. First, that pork tenderloin goes into a bag with olive oil, garlic, and a heavy palm of dried rosemary and thyme. Rub it now, let it sit overnight in the fridge. That's the difference between a crust and a dusting.
BUB: So the herbs actually stick to the meat?
BENDY: They bond. Also pull the chicken breasts and the beef stir-fry strips from the freezer and put them in the fridge to thaw slow. Chop one head of cauliflower into rice-sized pieces, and grab a second bag of pre-riced cauliflower for back-up. Slice an onion and a bag of mushrooms, keep them in separate containers.
BUB: I'm not eating mushrooms, but I'll chop them.
BENDY: Deal. Now Sunday. That tenderloin goes on the Traeger at 225 for about 45 minutes, until the internal temp hits 135. Pull it, tent it with foil for ten minutes—it will climb to 145 while you roast the Brussels sprouts and apples in a 400-degree oven. A little maple syrup and Dijon on the apples before they bake. They'll turn jammy at the edges.
BUB: Is the inside of the pork still pink? Because that's weird.
BENDY: It's pinkish and juicy, not raw. Trust the thermometer, not your eyes. Monday is the slow cooker soup. Here's the one move: do not add the cream until the last 20 minutes, or it will split and look like curdled milk. You're adding cauliflower rice at the very end too, so it stays with a bite and doesn't turn to mush.
BUB: So the soup gets the cream when the carrots are already soft?
BENDY: Exactly. Tuesday, beef and broccoli stir-fry on high heat. Get your pan screaming hot, then add the beef in a single layer. If you crowd it, it steams and turns gray. Broccoli goes in next, then a splash of water, and you cover it for one minute—that makes the stems bright green and slightly crisp.
BUB: Why zucchini noodles? Are we hiding vegetables?
BENDY: No, they just taste lighter than pasta. They only need two minutes at the end, otherwise they go watery. Wednesday is sausage, white bean, and kale soup. Use spicy Italian sausage and don't boil the kale. Add it in the last five minutes, stir it in until it just wilts. It stays deep green instead of turning into a muddy rag.
BUB: What about delicata squash? I saw it at the market.
BENDY: Good eye. Slice it into half-moons and roast it on the sheet pan right next to the soup pot. It's the side dish and you'll thank yourself. Thursday is the honey sesame chicken in the slow cooker. Make the sauce now—soy, honey, garlic, a little sriracha—and refrigerate it. It will keep and the flavors marry.
BUB: So Thursday we just dump it in the pot?
BENDY: And walk away for six hours. Then shred the chicken and toss it with cauliflower rice. Friday is the remix: leftover honey sesame chicken, chopped lettuce, sliced cucumber, and a squeeze of lime. No reheating. Just a cold salad that feels like a different meal.
BUB: So the sauce on Thursday is also the dressing on Friday?
BENDY: You're learning. Saturday is takeout, because we earned it.
BUB: Can I have the leftover roasted apples?
BENDY: They'll be gone by Tuesday. See you at the market.
